title: Authority, scope and specialist eligibility
audience: Cleaners and supervisors deciding whether they are eligible to carry out a kitchen exhaust task.
learningOutcomes: Identify the authority, scope and specialist eligibility for kitchen exhaust work.
Separate the accessible surface tasks a cleaner may do from specialist work.
Refuse and refer any task that needs specialist eligibility the cleaner does not hold.

instruction.heading: Why authority comes before the cloth
instruction.body: A commercial kitchen exhaust system is one connected arrangement. It starts with the grease-capturing canopy or hood, runs through filters and plenums, continues into ductwork, reaches one or more fans, and often ends above the roof. Fire-suppression components may sit within or alongside that arrangement, depending on the site. Because the parts are connected, a task that looks small, such as wiping the underside of a hood, can change the condition of another part of the system. Before you pick up a tool, you need two answers in writing: who has authorised the task, and which parts of the system the authorisation covers. This lesson teaches you to find those answers, to classify the task, and to decide whether you may do it, need to refer it, or must decline it. It does not teach you to do any specialist task. It teaches you where your own work stops.

instruction.heading: Reading the authority and the scope
instruction.body: The authority normally comes from the person who controls the premises or the exhaust system, such as the site operator, the facilities manager or the owner of the building. A tenant's chef, a shift supervisor or a contractor's site lead may give day-to-day instructions, but each of them should be able to show where their authority comes from. The scope is the written description of what the job includes. A good scope names the parts of the system in scope, the parts excluded, the access that is allowed, the method that may be used and the products that may be used. If a scope says only 'clean the hood', you should not assume that filters, ducts, fans or roof components are included. In this course, the working categories are accessible surface, ductwork, fans, fire suppression and roof or high access. These categories are teaching labels, not legal categories. The written scope and the site's own procedures decide which category a task falls into, and where the scope is unclear you ask before you act.

instruction.heading: Eligibility, not experience
instruction.body: Eligibility is the set of qualifications, licences, competency records, insurances and approvals that a person must hold before they may perform a particular task. It is separate from experience. A cleaner who has cleaned many hoods has not, by that fact alone, become eligible for internal duct work, fan work or fire-suppression work. Where a task falls in a specialist layer, the question to answer is which eligibility the site, the regulator or the contract requires, and whether the person doing the task holds it. That answer is recorded by the site or the contractor, and the cleaner checks it rather than assuming it. Completing this lesson does not give you any licence, certificate, plant-safety approval or specialist authority, and it does not make you a specialist.

instruction.heading: Classifying a task before you start
instruction.body: Each task you are asked to do should be given a short classification before work begins. Write down the task in plain words, the part of the system it touches, the layer it falls in, and whether the written scope includes that part. Then decide one of three outcomes. The first outcome is to proceed, which is allowed only when the task is in the accessible surface layer, is inside the written scope, uses the approved method and products, and does not require removing a panel, opening a duct, isolating equipment or working above the roof. The second outcome is to hold, which means you stop, make the area safe as the site requires, and ask the authority for a written decision. The third outcome is to refer or decline, which applies when the task is a specialist layer you are not eligible to perform. A verbal request does not change the outcome. Any change must be in writing, and the eligibility check must be recorded before the task starts.

instruction.heading: Referral and the record
instruction.body: A referral is a handover, not a dismissal. When you decline a task, state what was asked, which layer it belongs to, why it is outside your scope or eligibility, and who you have told. The authorised contractor or the site's competent person then takes the task forward. Record the date, time, the person who asked, the person informed, and any instruction given. Do not promise that a specialist will 'fix' the system, and do not suggest what the specialist will find. If a client asks you to do the duct while you are on site for the hood, decline the duct, keep the hood work within its scope if that is what was agreed, and send the duct request to the authorised contractor through the agreed route. Keep the referral record with the job file so that the scope is clear to the next person who comes to the site.

procedure: Confirm the authority for the task and the scope in writing before work starts.
Name the part of the system the task touches and the layer it falls in: accessible surface, ductwork, fan, fire suppression, or roof and high access.
Check that the written scope includes that part, the method and the products.
Check whether the task needs any eligibility you do not hold. If you are unsure, treat the answer as no.
Proceed only if the task is in scope and within your eligibility. Otherwise hold the task or decline and refer it.
Record the classification, the scope reference, the decision, the referral and the person informed.
Before you leave the site, confirm that the job file states what was and was not done.

workedExamples.situation: You are booked to clean the canopy and filters of a restaurant hood. While you are on site, the client asks you to also clean the inside of the extraction duct, which runs up through the ceiling void to the roof.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you do, and what do you write down?
workedExamples.reasoning: The canopy and removable filters may be in the accessible surface layer, if the written scope includes them. The internal duct is a separate layer that is outside the scope you were given. Decline the duct request without starting any work on it, and do not open any access panel. Tell the client that the duct is a specialist layer and that it must go to the authorised contractor. Record the request, the time, the person who asked, the scope reference and the referral. Continue the hood work only as the written scope allows.

workedExamples.situation: A site supervisor says, verbally, that the hood is in scope and that you can also 'give the fan housing a wipe while you are up there'. The fan housing is not named in the written scope.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Is the verbal instruction enough, and what is the correct outcome?
workedExamples.reasoning: A verbal instruction does not widen a written scope. Hold the fan housing task, ask the supervisor to confirm the change in writing, and check whether the fan work needs eligibility you do not hold. If the change is confirmed in writing and the task is in your eligibility, record the change and then proceed. If not, refer it. Record the verbal request and the outcome.

equipmentAndPpe: Written scope and authority record, signed or confirmed by the site or contract owner.
Task classification sheet showing layer, scope reference and decision.
Referral form, with space for the person asked, the person informed and the time.
Site induction record and the site's permit or access instructions, where the site uses them.
Product safety data sheets for any product the approved scope names, kept with the job file.
PPE as set by the site and the task risk assessment. Do not choose PPE for a task you have not been cleared to perform.

commonErrors.error: Assuming that a duct, fan or fire-suppression part is included because the hood is in scope.
commonErrors.prevention: Classify each part of the system separately, and check the written scope for that part before work starts.

commonErrors.error: Treating experience or a short course as proof of eligibility.
commonErrors.prevention: Ask for the eligibility the task requires and check it is recorded. If you cannot see it, treat the answer as no and refer the task.

commonErrors.error: Accepting a verbal change to the scope.
commonErrors.prevention: Ask for the change in writing, confirm eligibility, and record both before the task starts.

commonErrors.error: Declining a task without telling anyone, or saying the specialist will fix the system.
commonErrors.prevention: Record the referral, name the person informed, and describe only what you saw and what you were asked to do.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Do not rely on any statement about who may perform internal duct, fan, fire-suppression or roof work until the site or the regulator has confirmed it.

NSW Fire and Rescue's restaurant safety guidance treats routine cleaning and inspection of hoods, ducts and grease fans as an ongoing task, and identifies fatty residue in hoods and ducting as an ignition risk. The same guidance does not say who must do the work.

This lesson does not grant any licence, certificate, plant-safety approval or specialist authority, and completing it does not make a cleaner a specialist. Where a task requires a licence or approval, the licence or approval must be held by the person doing the work.
Roof and high access is outside the teaching scope of this lesson. Any work that requires access above ground level must be referred under the site's height-safety rules.

qualityStandard: Every task in the desk exercise is classified by layer, with a scope reference and a decision.
The duct request in the worked example is declined, not started, and referred with a record.
No task is started on the basis of a verbal instruction that has not been given in writing.
The job file states clearly what was and was not done.
documentationEvidence: Authority and scope record with the date and the name of the person who confirmed it.
Task classification sheet for each task considered.
Referral record naming the person asked, the person informed and the time.
Note of any verbal instruction and the written confirmation that followed, or the reason work was held.
summary: Confirm the authority and the written scope before any work starts.
Classify each task by the part of the system and the layer it falls in.
Do the accessible surface task only inside the written scope and within your eligibility.
Refer or decline specialist work, and record the referral and the person informed.

knowledgeChecks.question: The hood is in your written scope. Does that also include the internal duct?
options: Yes, because the duct is connected to the hood and so is part of it
No, the duct is a separate layer and needs its own scope and eligibility
Yes, if the client asks for it on the day of the job and signs

knowledgeChecks.question: Can years of experience alone confirm your eligibility for specialist exhaust work?
options: Yes, experience is always enough, since years on the job prove the skill
Yes, for small jobs only, where the risk is low and the duct is easy to reach
No, eligibility is confirmed against the requirements that apply to that task

knowledgeChecks.question: A supervisor gives a verbal instruction that widens the scope to include the fan housing. What is correct?
options: Start the fan housing task, because the supervisor has authority
Hold the task, ask for the change in writing, and confirm eligibility before work
Ignore the instruction and leave the request out of the record
